summary:
Ember is a web dashboard that gathers NASA’s spacecraft and habitat fire-safety research in one place and ranks it for the habitat you are designing: a space station, a cabin, or a Moon or Mars base. Fire is one of the deadliest risks for a crew, and the air in future bases will hold more oxygen than Earth’s, which makes materials burn more easily. NASA has run key fire experiments, but the results are scattered across reports, and almost no flame tests exist for Moon or Mars gravity.

Our SI assistant answers fire-safety questions using the loaded NASA records. It cites its sources, labels general knowledge as such, and says when the evidence is thin. Users can ask by voice and hear the answer read back. A 3D fire simulation lets them change gravity, oxygen, airflow and material to see how a flame behaves.

Ember helps engineers, researchers and students find what is known, and shows exactly where new tests are most needed.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Ember collects NASA’s fire-safety research on spacecraft and habitats into one dashboard. You pick a habitat (space station, spacecraft cabin, Moon base, Mars base or pressurized rover), and the evidence is ranked for that habitat’s atmosphere and gravity. Each record shows its pressure, oxygen level, gravity, method and source link. The ranking also depends on the data available, the method quality and how recent the research is, and users can change those weights.

An SI assistant answers fire-safety questions from the loaded NASA records. It cites record IDs, labels general knowledge, and says when evidence is thin or may not transfer between microgravity, Moon, Mars and Earth conditions. Users can ask by voice (speech to text) and hear the answer read aloud (text to speech). A 3D fire simulation lets users change gravity, oxygen, airflow and material to see how a flame spreads.

What benefits does it have?

  • Engineers and researchers find relevant NASA fire results in seconds instead of searching many reports by hand.
  • Every answer points back to its source, so people can check it.
  • It shows where evidence is missing, mainly at Moon and Mars gravity.
  • Students and teachers can explore space fire safety interactively.
  • Voice input and output help crews with busy hands and anyone who finds typing hard.

What is the intended impact?
We want safer habitat design decisions and better-targeted research. By showing which conditions have been tested and which haven’t, Ember points researchers to the tests that matter most, such as NASA’s planned Moon-gravity experiment (FM2). Ember is a reference aid. It does not replace mission procedures or mission control.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Tailwind CSS for styling.
  • Canvas 2D and WebGL for the 3D fire simulation.
  • Node.js serverless functions hosted on Vercel, with the code on GitHub.
  • Claude Haiku 5.5, accessed through OpenRouter, for the SI assistant. The API key stays on the server.
  • Deepgram for speech to text and text to speech, with the browser’s built-in voice as a fallback.
  • An earlier prototype ran on Node-RED with the Gemini API.
  • Playwright and Chrome for testing.
  • NASA sources: NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS), the Physical Sciences Informatics system, Saffire, SAME and BASS experiment records, and NASA Safety and Mission Assurance case pages.
  • We used Claude to help write and test the code, and we are happy to say so openly.

How is our project creative?

  • It turns a pile of technical reports into a ranked, habitat-specific answer instead of another search box.
  • The assistant is designed to be honest. It separates what a source says from what it infers, and it names evidence gaps.
  • The simulation is a physics sandbox rather than a realistic picture. It focuses on how gravity, oxygen and airflow change flame behavior, and it is labeled a sketch where no flame photos exist.
  • The project has a voice, so people can ask and listen instead of reading.
  • The name fits the theme: Ember is the last glow of a fire, and it stands for Evidence Mapping of Burning in Extraterrestrial Regions.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Accuracy and trust: Answers must cite NASA records, and the assistant must never invent values.
  • Safety: It is a reference aid and says so clearly.
  • Data gaps: Almost no flame tests exist for Moon or Mars gravity, so the dashboard shows that instead of hiding it.
  • Accessibility: Voice input and output, and a dark, high-contrast design.
  • Security and cost: API keys stay on the server and out of the code, and answers are kept short to control cost.
  • Reliability: Retries, timeouts and a backup voice keep it working during a demo.
  • Future growth: Adding Moon-gravity results as they appear, expert review of findings, and a crew-ready app.
